item.title: Jensen Huang Really Liked Selling China Advanced AI Chips
item.description: This scandal is a really big deal.
item.dc:creator: Zvi Mowshowitz
item.content:encoded:
This scandal is a really big deal. Jensen Huang has resigned after multiple affairs came to light, one of them with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang who also helped smuggle billions in Nvidia chips, and another with a.

The most important scandal around Jensen Huang has been known for a long time to those paying attention.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia have for years treated America and the United States Government as adversaries.

They have compromised the integrity of our government, potentially quite broadly, as well as the national security of the United States of America.

When Jensen Huang chose to have a long-running affair with Alice Huang, he knew that she was central to the diversion of billions of dollars in high end AI chips to China.

The nice term we used to use for this, back when anyone seemed to care, was corruption. There is also the less nice term that we used to use for such things.

Even on Monday we learned of yet another covert influence operation by Nvidia to promote them selling chips to China in order to ‘ensure US, not Chinese-made chips, continue to dominate the AI market.’

After several days in which Alice Huang’s status as a Chinese spy was not in dispute, we now have pushback from various sources that Alice Huang may not have formally been a Chinese spy.

It is possible that she was not formally recruited, and did not share intel with the CCP. If true, this hopefully would mean there was not additional loss of intelligence or other things due to this relationship.

Trump is now saying he doesn’t know she’s a Chinese spy, after many days of (like everyone else) conspicuously not saying that.

So okay, now the arrow says ‘suspected of’ spying, out of an abundance of caution.

Does putting ‘suspected of’ there change the overall picture? Is that the only thing you should put in that arrow, as opposed to for example ‘smuggled chips for’?

(Also, this is missing the third ‘alleged’ affair. There’s always more stuff.)

Or this graph, originally from Bloomberg?

Even if it turns out she was not part of the formal Chinese spy network, she was acting as a de facto Chinese agent.

Nor does it change that he had three affairs that we know about, one of which was with a major customer illegally smuggling billions in chips and the other two with Nvidia employees including at least one direct report.

If you wish, you can retroactively qualify or modify all my related statements about Alice Huang accordingly.

Table of Contents

  1. The Story That Matters Most.

  2. Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening.

  3. How Far Does This Go?

  4. The First Step Is Admitting You Have a Problem.

  5. Somehow People Are Still Defending Jensen Huang.

  6. Jensen Huang Wants to Call It a Comeback.

  7. On Interim CEO Kress.

  8. An Actual Attack on Jensen’s Character.

  9. Solve for the New Equilibrium.

  10. But This Time They’ve Gone Too Far.

The Story That Matters Most

Miles Brundage is correct to draw the parallel to the situation with Jacob Coxon.

The reason I keep Mike Solana on as a source, despite all his rhetoric, is that underneath it all he calls it like he sees it, so we get statements like this one:

Yes Export Controls Matter and Are Finally Happening

Something about a goose chasing you asking why the stocks went down.

Jensen Huang no longer being CEO of Nvidia is crashing the value of Z.ai. Why?

You know exactly why.

We kept not getting new export controls because Howard Lutnick kept not allowing them to go forward, forcing Scott Bessent and the NSC to finally go around him in order to issue a remote access rule and to expand.

This way of getting the rule finalized was an unprecedented move, forced by unprecedented refusal to follow either the national interest or the wishes of the President.

We badly need these rules. Nvidia did not even cut off specifically Megaspeed, after they were caught and supposedly put on a ‘no sell’ list, to the extent that this was not even hidden from trade records:

Nvidia’s board may at least be pretending to do something about this, now. They have announced a new Oversights Committee. That’ll fix it.

How Far Does This Go?

As Nate Silver says, this story is a really big deal. He argues that the political world, partly due to this being a busy news cycle, is still underreacting to this story.

Potentially this goes all the way to the top. Congress will be investigating.

There is a strong case that this is the most serious scandal of the Trump era, full stop.

It almost certainly goes as far as Howard Lutnick. Hopefully Lutnick gets removed.

Straight up corruption is a plausible hypothesis.

Potentially it could reach David Sacks, who was the AI Czar and in that position was very clearly de facto functioning as Nvidia’s chief lobbyist and advocate.

The First Step Is Admitting You Have a Problem

I find this part of the story very much to Huang’s credit.

Alas, he loses most of that credit the minute he starts planning a potential comeback.

Somehow People Are Still Defending Jensen Huang

There is a logic that goes something like this, and it generalizes beyond Huang:

  1. Jensen Huang did these no good, quite bad things, sure.

  2. But they never would have come to light like this, and he would have gotten away with it, except for those meddling kids, who told the truth about it.

  3. Thus this is character assassination, a government plot, tyranny, must not stand.

This comes from a cultural position that of course anyone powerful will have done many horrible things, and of course we do not hold them accountable, so trying to hold them accountable by saying the things they have.

I disagree.

There are also arguments that take this form:

  1. Jensen Huang was the founder and CEO.

  2. Therefore, Nvidia is his, and if you take it away from him, you need proof that he did something sufficiently horrible, and it’s like a court of law.

  3. But you can’t formally prove the exact thing in question, so he walks, which means you have to let him continue to run Nvidia. This is an outrage.

  4. I mean, come on, OpenAI’s board couldn’t fire Sam Altman, and also I would really like if my board couldn’t fire me. So let’s bring Jensen Huang back.

No, seriously. As in:

Again, I disagree. This is madness.

The central purpose of the board of directors is to, if necessary, fire the CEO.

You also have this great illustration of a deeply twisted worldview twice over:

China does not want Jensen Huang out, or at least I would be extremely surprised and confused to learn that China wanted that.

Then there’s the second level. Why do you think it is a good argument, or virtuous, or that it speaks well of you, to publicly say that you want Jensen in because China wants him out?

Which in turn makes you make up stuff about what the other guy wants.

I like to think Palmer Luckey does not actually think like that, and instead only thinks that it is beneficial to his social position to present himself as thinking like this, and thus is lying.

Teortaxes tries to maintain that what ‘has been done’ to Jensen is 'significantly worse than what happened to Jack Ma.’ Nothing ‘was done’ to Jensen other than to reveal things he most.

I thought all of that was as crazy as it would get. Boy was I wrong. I happened to see this post by Ben Thompson, ‘Obituaries,’ in which he calls this the death of, and I swear I am not making this up:

  1. Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, okay, I guess.

  2. Nvidia, most valuable company in the world, not technically accurate, but ok.

  3. The AI bubble, ‘2025-2027’, ?!, sigh.

  4. AI as normal technology and the US Semiconductor industry, 1947-2047, ???.

  5. Tech company independence, 1968-2026, no, seriously.

  6. American exceptionalism, 1776-2026, no, seriously.

What does one even say to something like that, when what happened was ‘tech CEO who treated America as an adversary and facilitated the smuggling of billions in chips while sleeping with the executive in question.

If this is the end of American exceptionalism or tech company independence, what about [unfurls comically long scroll of events from the second Trump administration, the Biden administration, the first Trump.

Max Read is on point on why some people cannot let this one go, no matter how obviously Jensen Huang is now unfit to be CEO of Nvidia, and how badly this compromised national security.

To those in the vibe army of the Silicon Valley founder class, they are visionaries who will save the world. Any limits whatsoever on their power, any attempt to impose any form of control on them, is tyranny.

The China dove part is obvious. The weird part about it is that the main reason to be a China dove is so that Nvidia can sell more chips and thus make more money.

This is then piled on top of the open weight support. Jensen Huang supports open weights, not out of ideology but because he wants to commoditize his complement and does not understand the nature of the risks involved.

If I was in the AI or tech industry and thinking strategically, I would not want to make it look like the tech industry was rallying around Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang Wants to Call It a Comeback

He has discussed this potential comeback with allies.

One of those allies is Gavin Baker, calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement, including supporting his reinstatement now pending the investigation.

They also arranged for a letter warning that ‘irreplaceable’ talent could be lost if Jensen Huang is not reinstated. There are always such warnings, and indeed some employees do leave when the CEO changes.

These people are even betting that this could happen. As in, see Polymarket, where people are buying Jensen Huang remaining as CEO at 16% (!?):

No, sir. This is not going to happen. Even if the board were somehow willing to cave on this, and even if Trump says otherwise and is saying Huang 'learned a big lesson,’ the rest of Washington is absolutely not.

The board, knowing this and also for other very good reasons, is having none of it.

This is the kind of thing that makes DC think that the tech industry is completely clueless and also hostile and dangerous. They flat out don’t get it.

Or maybe I am the one who is wrong, because it is 2026 and literally nothing matters.

There are plenty of out of line actions to go around. Donald Trump was out of line and being deeply silly to suggest a specific person, Tim Cook, take over Nvidia.

As Joe Weisenthal says, can you imagine if Elizabeth Warren was the one saying that?

But also, the man has a point. If your company facilitates this level of blatantly illegal activity on matters vital to national security, I can see why you might need an outsider.

OpenAI and Anthropic and SpaceX and Meta and so on have these different special governing structures, in theory or in practice, part of which is to make the CEO harder to fire.

The board might try to not fire Elon Musk in a similar situation. Good luck with that.

If I was Jensen Huang, I would be less worried about trying to return as CEO and more worried about cooperation, and the potential civil and criminal implications, and hopefully also I would care about national security.

On Interim CEO Kress

I agree with Joe’s interpretation here of WSJ’s description of events.

Jensen Huang’s style was highly abrasive. I think the WSJ article was painting this disagreement into something that it was not, and that it does not provide much evidence of Jensen Huang’s central opinions.

An Actual Attack on Jensen’s Character

Yes, if you are quietly tipping waitresses $1,000 you are not doing it as an Effective Altruist. You are largely doing it because you feel great doing it.

The part that matters is the second half, and given what I’ve seen on podcasts I have little doubt that Witt is accurate here:

This kind of ‘cult of the great man’ reaction is understandable in the face of the whiplash here, but neglects that Witt claims very strong direct evidence.

We also have this article about Put-Downs, Parties and a ‘Royal Family.’

I mean, yes, of course you put the company above any person. Or at least any person other than yourself. That’s how it works.

And if the CEO tells you to try the brisket? You try the brisket.

Whiplash is a great movie. The instructor is, in my view, neither hero nor villain. He simply is who he is, as is the student.

Solve for the New Equilibrium

I see why Dean Ball is taking the contrary position, but I fear that he is wrong.

The current situation is that many people, including very powerful people but also many ordinary people, have a bunch of secrets that could harm them quite a bit if weaponized.

There are also any number of pieces of true information (e.g. your banking password) that you would very much not want others to know, even if you are doing nothing wrong.

I think of this as analogous to cyber. Offense generally defeats defense under realistic conditions, because offense can concentrate firepower.

But This Time They’ve Gone Too Far

I do want to stand up for Jensen Huang in at least this small way: His plaque.

That action, in particular, is an outrage, assuming the story is true. This man earned that plaque.

Let us not take away from Jensen Huang his thirty-three year history of building Nvidia. There would be no Nvidia, certainly not in anything like its present form, without the efforts of Jensen Huang.

He is also responsible for his own downfall, and for choosing to sell so many chips to China when there was other demand for them, and for intentionally leaving Nvidia without an easy succession path.

Let us remember him for all of it.
